title: Study Maps Shapes and Colours of Near-Death Experiences
excerpt: Researchers mapped the spaces 50 people recalled from near-death experiences, finding most tunnel-like scenes were colourless.
content:
Live Poll

Do you believe the brain alone can fully explain near-death experiences?

A study in Frontiers in Psychology, led by Dr France Lerner of the University of Haifa in Israel, mapped the spatial shapes and colours of near-death experiences reported by 50 people. Participants recalled their experiences around 15 years earlier and drew them using guided online sessions with geometric shapes.

Why it matters

Near-death experiences are reported by an estimated 1 in 12 people, so structured records of what those experiences look like add to a field that has relied largely on verbal accounts. Mapping recalled scenes into consistent categories gives researchers a way to compare reports across individuals.

Of 28 tunnel-like spaces described by 50 participants, 22 were colourless, while 27 of 31 broad curved spaces were recalled in colour. The reason for this split is not addressed in the study details available.

The players

Dr France Lerner

Dr France Lerner is a neurophenomenology researcher at the University of Haifa in Israel who led the study.

University of Haifa

The University of Haifa is a public research university in Haifa, Israel, and the home institution of the study's lead researcher.

The details

Participants mapped each stage of their experience using a set of geometric shapes, marking where they were, how they moved, and what colours they saw. Most scenes fell into four categories: cone-shaped spaces, broad curved spaces, flatter gently curving spaces, and spheres or ovals surrounding the observer.

Timeline

  1. Participants had their near-death experiences around 15 years before the study.

  2. The study was published on 20 November 2026.

Research Landscape

Dutch cardiologist Dr Pim van Lommel, who was not involved in this study, has previously reported that almost 1 in 4 cardiac arrest survivors recalled a near-death experience. This new work shifts the focus from what people report to how they spatially recall those scenes.

Readers who have survived cardiac arrest or been close to death may find these findings useful for understanding how memories of such experiences are formed. The study does not offer treatment or clinical guidance.

The takeaway

Near-death experiences can be recorded in structured ways that reveal consistent patterns in how people remember them. Those patterns offer a starting point for comparing accounts across different people and studies.
